title: Prescriptions from Out-of-State Practitioners
subtopic: Three pathways, their windows, and the duties each places on the pharmacist
learning_objectives: Identify which of the three out-of-state pathways the facts fall into before reaching for any number.
Apply the correct presentation window: 30 days for schedules III through VI, 5 days for either schedule II route.
Apply the authenticity duty to every pathway and the telephone-verification duty to the pathways that carry it.
Separate the window on the prescription from the five-day limit on an initial partial dispensing.
Carry out the post-fill reporting duty the schedule II pathways impose.

orientation.text: Massachusetts does not have one out-of-state rule; it has three, and they sit in adjacent subsections of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18. Subsection (c) covers schedules III through VI issued by an authorized practitioner licensed and registered where they reside or practise. Subsection (d) covers a NONNARCOTIC schedule II prescription from an out-of-state practitioner. Subsection (d1/2) covers a NARCOTIC schedule II prescription, and narrows the issuing states to Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth. The first question on any out-of-state fact pattern is which of the three you are in, because the window and the duties both change.

The windows are the easy half. A schedule III through VI prescription may be filled here only if it was issued within the preceding 30 days. Either schedule II route runs on five days instead. Neither window is a federal clock: the federal six-month schedule III and IV period does not license a prescription Massachusetts no longer treats as fillable, because the presentation window is the earlier gate and it closes first.

The duties are where candidates go wrong. Every one of the three subsections places a duty on the FILLING PHARMACIST to determine, in accordance with professional standards and personal judgment, that the prescription is authentic and valid. On top of that, subsection (c) adds telephone or other verification only where the substance is in schedules III to V, while subsections (d) and (d1/2) each state the verification duty independently for their schedule II routes. The practical shape is counter-intuitive: verification is NOT a schedule III to V speciality, and schedule VI is the single pathway that carries the authenticity duty without it. On every pathway a pharmacist shall not fill a prescription for which verification cannot be obtained, and is protected from liability for refusing where good faith efforts were documented.

Two duties survive the fill itself. If the prescription is a schedule II filled under (d) or (d1/2), the pharmacist must deliver a copy to the Department within 30 days of the FILLING, with the patient's name and address removed. And if such a prescription is partially dispensed, a separate five-day limit governs the initial partial dispensing while the remainder still closes 30 days after the issue date. Two different five-day rules therefore live in this area, one about when the prescription may be presented and one about when an initial partial dispensing must be completed.

worked_examples.scenario: A New Hampshire physician's written prescription for amphetamine salts, a nonnarcotic Schedule II substance, is presented at your Massachusetts pharmacy three days after it was issued. The prescriber is registered in New Hampshire and under federal law. Your technician says verification is only needed for Schedules III through V. What do you do?
steps: Identify the pathway. A nonnarcotic Schedule II from an out-of-state practitioner is M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d), not s. 18(c) and not the narcotic route in s. 18(d1/2).
Check the window. s. 18(d) authorizes filling only where the prescription was issued within the preceding five days; three days is inside it.

Apply the duty the pathway states. s. 18(d) requires the filling pharmacist both to determine authenticity and validity in accordance with professional standards and personal judgment and to verify the prescription by telephone or other means. The technician is wrong: verification is not a Schedule III through V speciality.
If verification cannot be obtained, do not fill. Document the good faith efforts; the statute protects a pharmacist who refuses on that basis.
After filling, start the post-fill clock: a copy goes to the Department within 30 days of the filling, without the patient's name and address.
worked_examples.resolution: Verify before filling. Skipping verification here would fill a Schedule II prescription without a step s. 18(d) makes a precondition of the fill, and the Department copy is still owed 30 days after the filling.

worked_examples.scenario: A Connecticut nurse practitioner's prescription for a Schedule VI antihypertensive is presented 20 days after issue. Your colleague wants to telephone the prescriber's office to verify before filling, and is frustrated that nobody is answering after hours. Must the fill wait for that call?
steps: Identify the pathway. Schedule VI from an out-of-state practitioner falls under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), which reaches schedules III to VI inclusive.
Check the window. s. 18(c) authorizes filling a prescription issued within the preceding 30 days; 20 days is inside it.

Read the duty precisely. s. 18(c) imposes the authenticity-and-validity determination on every prescription it reaches, but conditions telephone or other verification on the substance being in schedules III to V. Schedule VI is outside that condition.

So the pharmacist still has to be satisfied, in accordance with professional standards and personal judgment, that the prescription is authentic and valid -- but the separate telephone-verification duty is not triggered.
worked_examples.resolution: No. The fill does not wait on a verification call that this pathway does not require. Schedule VI is the one out-of-state pathway carrying the authenticity duty without the telephone-verification duty, and this is the distinction the wording of s. 18(c) turns on.

worked_examples.scenario: A Rhode Island physician's oxycodone prescription, a Schedule II narcotic, is presented four days after issue. The patient asks for only part of the quantity today. Which five-day rule are you applying, and what closes when?
steps: Identify the pathway. A narcotic Schedule II from a contiguous state is s. 18(d1/2), and Rhode Island is contiguous with the commonwealth.
The first five-day rule is the presentation window: s. 18(d1/2) authorizes filling only where the prescription was issued within the preceding five days. Four days is inside it.
Verify the prescription by telephone or other means, and do not fill if verification cannot be obtained.

The second five-day rule is different: the initial partial dispensing of a prescription filled pursuant to s. 18(d) or (d1/2) must be filled not more than five days after the prescription issue date. That also lands on day five, but it is measuring the dispensing rather than the presentation.
The remaining portion runs on its own clock: not later than 30 days after the issue date, and only at the same pharmacy that dispensed the lesser quantity.
worked_examples.resolution: Both five-day rules are satisfied today, and they are not the same rule. Note the partial dispensing and quantity in the patient record, keep any remainder at this pharmacy, complete it within 30 days of the issue date, and send the anonymised Department copy within 30 days of the filling.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which out-of-state pathway carries the authenticity duty but NOT the telephone-verification duty, and why?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Schedule VI under s. 18(c). The subsection reaches schedules III to VI but conditions verification on the substance being in schedules III to V.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Out-of-state presentation windows: schedules III through VI, ______ days; either schedule II route, ______ days.
True or false: verification by telephone or other means is required only for out-of-state schedule III through V prescriptions.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) each state the verification duty independently for the nonnarcotic and narcotic schedule II routes.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which states may issue a narcotic Schedule II prescription fillable in Massachusetts under the out-of-state pathway?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Maine, or a state contiguous with the commonwealth.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A pharmacist refuses an out-of-state prescription because verification could not be obtained. What protects them, and what is the condition?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The statute provides they shall not be held liable for the refusal, provided documented good faith efforts were made to determine authenticity and validity.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The Department copy after filling an out-of-state Schedule II prescription is due within ______, measured from ______, and must omit ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: 30 days; the filling; the patient's name and address.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the two distinct five-day rules in this area.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The presentation window for a schedule II prescription under s. 18(d) or (d1/2), and the limit on completing an initial partial dispensing of such a prescription.

quick_review.text: An authorized out-of-state practitioner's schedule III through VI prescription may be filled in Massachusetts only if it was issued within the preceding 30 days.
Massachusetts applies a five-day presentation window to out-of-state schedule II prescriptions instead, under separate subsections with their own issuing-state conditions.
The schedule II narcotic route reaches only a practitioner registered in Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth.

Every out-of-state pathway requires the filling pharmacist to determine authenticity and validity; telephone verification is additionally required on schedules III through V and on both schedule II routes, leaving schedule VI as the one pathway without it.
Where the out-of-state prescription is oral and in schedules III through V, the pharmacist records having requested the practitioner's written prescription.
A prescription filled under s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2) has its own five-day limit on the INITIAL PARTIAL DISPENSING, separate from the window on presenting the prescription.
After filling an out-of-state schedule II prescription the pharmacist delivers a copy to the Department within 30 days, with the patient's name and address removed.

decision_logic.condition: An out-of-state practitioner's prescription is presented.
decision_logic.action: Identify the subsection first: schedules III through VI run on s. 18(c) and 30 days, a nonnarcotic schedule II on s. 18(d) and five days, a narcotic schedule II on s. 18(d1/2), five days and a narrower list of issuing states.

decision_logic.condition: You have identified the pathway and the prescription is inside its window.
decision_logic.action: Determine, in accordance with professional standards and personal judgment, that the prescription is authentic and valid. Then verify by telephone or other means unless the substance is schedule VI, and do not fill if verification cannot be obtained.
Refuse the fill and document the good faith efforts made; the statute protects the refusal on that basis.

decision_logic.condition: The out-of-state schedule III-V prescription was communicated orally.
decision_logic.action: Record that you requested the practitioner deliver or mail the written prescription within seven days or the shorter federal period.

decision_logic.condition: An out-of-state schedule II prescription under s. 18(d) or (d1/2) is partially dispensed.
decision_logic.action: Complete the initial partial dispensing not more than five days after the issue date, keep any remainder at this pharmacy, and fill it not later than 30 days after the issue date.

decision_logic.condition: You have filled an out-of-state schedule II prescription.
decision_logic.action: Deliver a copy to the Department within 30 days of the filling, excluding the patient's name and address.

ma_vs_federal.text: The federal six-month schedule III and IV clock does not license an out-of-state prescription that Massachusetts no longer treats as fillable; the presentation window is the earlier gate.
The out-of-state oral schedule III through V follow-up period is stated as seven days or the shorter period federal law requires, so a shorter federal period governs where one exists.

exceptions.text: The five-day schedule II window sits in separate subsections that also carry their own conditions on which issuing states qualify, so it is not simply a shorter version of the same rule.
Separate delivery provisions govern certain out-of-state residents, so the narcotic route is not simply the nonnarcotic route with a different list of states.
Schedule VI is the one out-of-state pathway carrying the authenticity duty without the separate telephone-verification duty.

The out-of-state schedule II subsections authorize the filling only. They do not authorize the practitioner to possess, administer or dispense controlled substances in the commonwealth or to practise here, and they do not authorize mail order pharmacies.

timing_deadlines.event: Out-of-state schedule III through VI prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: Outside the window this pathway does not authorize the fill at all.

timing_deadlines.event: Out-of-state schedule II prescription, either route
timing_deadlines.consequence: The 30-day figure does not carry across to schedule II.

timing_deadlines.event: Initial partial dispensing of an out-of-state schedule II prescription
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 5 days after the prescription issue date
timing_deadlines.consequence: This limit governs the dispensing, not the presentation.

timing_deadlines.event: Remaining portion of that partially dispensed prescription
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not later than 30 days after the prescription issue date
timing_deadlines.consequence: The remainder closes on the issue-date clock and only at the same pharmacy.

timing_deadlines.event: Practitioner delivery of an out-of-state oral schedule III-V written follow-up
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within 7 days or the shorter federal period
timing_deadlines.consequence: The period governs the practitioner's delivery, not the pharmacist's recording.

timing_deadlines.event: Department copy after filling an out-of-state schedule II prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: This clock runs from the filling, unlike every other period in this section.

forms_records.text: On the out-of-state oral schedule III-V pathway the pharmacist records having requested the practitioner's written prescription.
An initial partial dispensing and any remainder carry the s. 18(d3/4) patient-record notation of the partial fill and the quantity dispensed, accessible to the prescriber on request.
The Department copy excludes the patient's name and address, and neither the copy nor its contents is a public record.
Where verification cannot be obtained, the good faith efforts made are themselves the record that protects the refusal.

role_duties.duty: Determine authenticity and validity on every out-of-state pathway, and verify by telephone or other means on every pathway except schedule VI.
Refuse to fill an out-of-state prescription for which verification cannot be obtained.
Deliver the anonymised Department copy within 30 days of filling an out-of-state schedule II prescription.

common_traps.text: Treating verification as a schedule III through V feature fills an out-of-state nonnarcotic schedule II prescription without a step s. 18(d) makes a precondition of the fill.
Carrying the 30-day out-of-state window to a schedule II prescription accepts one that Massachusetts allows only within five days of issue.
Filling an out-of-state schedule III-V prescription on the federal six-month clock skips both the presentation window and the verification gate.
Treating the seven-day follow-up period as the pharmacist's deadline reverses the timed event.
Reading the five-day figure as one rule merges the window on presenting the prescription with the separate limit on completing an initial partial dispensing.
Measuring the Department copy's 30 days from the issue date rather than from the filling misses that this is the one duty here keyed to the dispensing event.
Demanding a verification call on a schedule VI out-of-state prescription applies a duty s. 18(c) conditions on schedules III to V.
